sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Rebecca Parlakian, 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: We often insist that our toddlers say "I'm sorry" as a way for them to take responsibility for their actions. But many toddlers don't fully understand what these words mean. ... While it may feel "right" for them to say "I'm sorry", it doesn't necessarily help toddlers learn empathy. ... A more meaningful approach can be to help children focus on the other person's feelings: ... Chandra, look at Sierra—she's very sad. She's crying. ... This helps children make the connection between the action (shoving) and the reaction (a friend who is sad and crying). ... Read stories about feelings. Some suggestions include:
sources.supports: Insisting on the words does not necessarily teach empathy (the page is about toddlers); pointing out the other child's feelings helps connect action and reaction; reading stories about feelings is one of its suggestions. Applied here to older children as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Steps to Teaching Kids to Say “I’m Sorry”
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Lindsey Pruett-Hornbaker, 18 May 2021
sources.quote: One of the best ways to help young children learn empathy is to ask wondering questions about other people’s feelings. ... When we ask our kids to say they’re sorry, what we are truly asking them to do is to take responsibility. ... When we offer to help fix the problem, we let other people know we care about them. ... I’m sorry. I can tell that makes you sad and didn’t mean to hurt you! How can I help?
sources.supports: Wondering questions about the other child's feelings, an apology as taking responsibility, offering to help fix the problem, and the wording of a real apology that ends with an offer to help. A US public media page for parents, used as general advice.

sources.title: “I'm Sorry:” Apologizing to Your Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Rebecca Parlakian, 10 Sep 2015
sources.quote: clearly states what the adult did wrong in simple terms that a child can understand ... I yelled at you and I shouldn't; I'm sorry for that. ... I'm sorry for yelling, but your tantrum got me really upset. ... how to take responsibility for their actions and how to forgive
sources.supports: A true apology names what was done wrong in simple words and has no 'but'; when parents apologise like this they model it for the child. Used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Rebecca Parlakian, 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: We often insist that our toddlers say "I'm sorry" as a way for them to take responsibility for their actions. But many toddlers don't fully understand what these words mean. ... While it may feel "right" for them to say "I'm sorry", it doesn't necessarily help toddlers learn empathy. ... A more meaningful approach can be to help children focus on the other person's feelings: ... Chandra, look at Sierra—she's very sad. She's crying. ... This helps children make the connection between the action (shoving) and the reaction (a friend who is sad and crying). ... Read stories about feelings. Some suggestions include:
sources.supports: Insisting on the words does not necessarily teach empathy (the page is about toddlers); pointing out the other child's feelings helps connect action and reaction; reading stories about feelings is one of its suggestions. Applied here to older children as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Steps to Teaching Kids to Say “I’m Sorry”
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Lindsey Pruett-Hornbaker, 18 May 2021
sources.quote: One of the best ways to help young children learn empathy is to ask wondering questions about other people’s feelings. ... When we ask our kids to say they’re sorry, what we are truly asking them to do is to take responsibility. ... When we offer to help fix the problem, we let other people know we care about them. ... I’m sorry. I can tell that makes you sad and didn’t mean to hurt you! How can I help?
sources.supports: Wondering questions about the other child's feelings, an apology as taking responsibility, offering to help fix the problem, and the wording of a real apology that ends with an offer to help. A US public media page for parents, used as general advice.

sources.title: “I'm Sorry:” Apologizing to Your Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Rebecca Parlakian, 10 Sep 2015
sources.quote: clearly states what the adult did wrong in simple terms that a child can understand ... I yelled at you and I shouldn't; I'm sorry for that. ... I'm sorry for yelling, but your tantrum got me really upset. ... how to take responsibility for their actions and how to forgive
sources.supports: A true apology names what was done wrong in simple words and has no 'but'; when parents apologise like this they model it for the child. Used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Rebecca Parlakian, 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: We often insist that our toddlers say "I'm sorry" as a way for them to take responsibility for their actions. But many toddlers don't fully understand what these words mean. ... While it may feel "right" for them to say "I'm sorry", it doesn't necessarily help toddlers learn empathy. ... A more meaningful approach can be to help children focus on the other person's feelings: ... Chandra, look at Sierra—she's very sad. She's crying. ... This helps children make the connection between the action (shoving) and the reaction (a friend who is sad and crying). ... Read stories about feelings. Some suggestions include:
sources.supports: Insisting on the words does not necessarily teach empathy (the page is about toddlers); pointing out the other child's feelings helps connect action and reaction; reading stories about feelings is one of its suggestions. Applied here to older children as general advice.

sources.title: 5 Steps to Teaching Kids to Say “I’m Sorry”
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Lindsey Pruett-Hornbaker, 18 May 2021
sources.quote: One of the best ways to help young children learn empathy is to ask wondering questions about other people’s feelings. ... When we ask our kids to say they’re sorry, what we are truly asking them to do is to take responsibility. ... When we offer to help fix the problem, we let other people know we care about them. ... I’m sorry. I can tell that makes you sad and didn’t mean to hurt you! How can I help?
sources.supports: Wondering questions about the other child's feelings, an apology as taking responsibility, offering to help fix the problem, and the wording of a real apology that ends with an offer to help. A US public media page for parents, used as general advice.

sources.title: “I'm Sorry:” Apologizing to Your Child
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Rebecca Parlakian, 10 Sep 2015

sources.title: Frustration Tolerance
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (5 Mar 2009)
sources.quote: break the challenge into manageable parts ... let them know that you appreciate how difficult it can be ... Puzzles are hard! ... become their coach ... help them think through solutions without doing the work for them
sources.supports: Saying out loud that the task is hard, breaking it into manageable parts, and coaching instead of doing it for the child. Used as general advice for young children.

sources.title: Stick With It: Encouraging Persistence in Kids
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Rebecca Parlakian, 15 Dec 2021
sources.quote: This can’t happen if adults rescue them at the first hint of difficulty. ... try the 15-20 piece puzzle and see what happens. ... Would you like to take a break or have a little help?
sources.supports: Children learn to persist by working through obstacles, which does not happen when adults rescue them at the first hint of difficulty; offering a break or a little help when frustration peaks. Used as general advice.

sources.title: Encouraging Your Child to Keep Trying
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), 2 Jul 2015
sources.quote: Persistence is about helping your child move from “I can’t do it” to “I can’t do it yet — I’m learning!” ... “I know you can do this. Let’s take a break and have a snack. Then you can come back and try again.” ... let them know that, win or lose, we are proud of them for their effort.
sources.supports: The words 'I can't do it yet, I'm learning', a break and a snack before trying again, and being proud of the effort win or lose. Used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Rebecca Parlakian, 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: We often insist that our toddlers say "I'm sorry" as a way for them to take responsibility for their actions. But many toddlers don't fully understand what these words mean. ... While it may feel "right" for them to say "I'm sorry", it doesn't necessarily help toddlers learn empathy. ... A more meaningful approach can be to help children focus on the other person's feelings: ... Chandra, look at Sierra—she's very sad. She's crying. ... This helps children make the connection between the action (shoving) and the reaction (a friend who is sad and crying). ... Read stories about feelings. Some suggestions include:
sources.supports: Insisting on the words does not necessarily teach empathy (the page is about toddlers); pointing out the other child's feelings helps connect action and reaction; reading stories about feelings is one of its suggestions. Applied here to older children as general advice.

sources.title: Stick With It: Encouraging Persistence in Kids
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), Rebecca Parlakian, 15 Dec 2021
sources.quote: This can’t happen if adults rescue them at the first hint of difficulty. ... try the 15-20 piece puzzle and see what happens. ... Would you like to take a break or have a little help?
sources.supports: Children learn to persist by working through obstacles, which does not happen when adults rescue them at the first hint of difficulty; offering a break or a little help when frustration peaks. Used as general advice.

sources.title: Frustration Tolerance
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (5 Mar 2009)
sources.quote: break the challenge into manageable parts ... let them know that you appreciate how difficult it can be ... Puzzles are hard! ... become their coach ... help them think through solutions without doing the work for them
sources.supports: Saying out loud that the task is hard, breaking it into manageable parts, and coaching instead of doing it for the child. Used as general advice for young children.

sources.title: Encouraging Your Child to Keep Trying
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Public Broadcasting Service), 2 Jul 2015
sources.quote: Persistence is about helping your child move from “I can’t do it” to “I can’t do it yet — I’m learning!” ... “I know you can do this. Let’s take a break and have a snack. Then you can come back and try again.” ... let them know that, win or lose, we are proud of them for their effort.
sources.supports: The words 'I can't do it yet, I'm learning', a break and a snack before trying again, and being proud of the effort win or lose. Used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (Rebecca Parlakian, 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: We often insist that our toddlers say "I'm sorry" as a way for them to take responsibility for their actions. But many toddlers don't fully understand what these words mean. ... While it may feel "right" for them to say "I'm sorry", it doesn't necessarily help toddlers learn empathy. ... A more meaningful approach can be to help children focus on the other person's feelings: ... Chandra, look at Sierra—she's very sad. She's crying. ... This helps children make the connection between the action (shoving) and the reaction (a friend who is sad and crying). ... Read stories about feelings. Some suggestions include:
sources.supports: Insisting on the words does not necessarily teach empathy (the page is about toddlers); pointing out the other child's feelings helps connect action and reaction; reading stories about feelings is one of its suggestions. Applied here to older children as general advice.
